### Step 6: Verify Commit Readiness

**Purpose**: Final checklist before committing

**Checklist**:
```markdown
□ Only files with public value are staged
□ Internal development artifacts excluded
□ Non-conventional files skipped
□ All related changes staged together
□ Commit message follows Conventional Commits format
□ Message is clear to external developers (no jargon)
□ No sensitive information (passwords, keys, tokens)
□ Changes are logically grouped (atomic commit)
□ Tests pass (if applicable)
```

**Actions**:
```bash
# Review staged changes
git diff --cached

# Check commit message
git commit -v  # Opens editor with diff

# Or commit directly
git commit -m "type(scope): description" -m "Body explaining why"
```

**Validation**: `commit_ready`

### Step 7: Scoped-Staging Discipline (Dirty Working Tree)

**Purpose**: Prevent sweeping someone else's in-flight WIP into YOUR commit when the working tree is dirty (unrelated uncommitted or already-staged changes belonging to another packet/agent).

**Why this matters (real incident)**: During a large spec-folder reorg, an orchestrator ran a broad `git add` while the tree held unrelated WIP. 24 unrelated files (another packet plus install guides) were swept into the reorg commit and had to be backed out with `git reset --mixed HEAD~1` and re-staged precisely. See `shared-patterns.md` §10 for the rename-heavy merge half of the same incident.

**Hard rules**:

- **NEVER** use `git add -A`, `git add .`, or a broad `git add <folder>` when the tree contains unrelated uncommitted or staged changes. These sweep everything, including another agent's WIP and already-staged index entries.
- Stage **explicit pathspecs for YOUR change only**. Enumerate the files; do not stage by directory unless every file under it is yours.
- Some unrelated WIP may already be **staged** (in the index) before you start. A broad add is not required to capture it — it is already captured. You MUST inspect the index, not just the unstaged diff.

**Step 6a: Snapshot the tree before staging**:
```bash
git status --short                 # See BOTH staged (left col) and unstaged (right col)
git diff --cached --name-only      # Exactly what is ALREADY in the index
```
If `git diff --cached --name-only` is non-empty and those files are not yours, decide first: unstage them (`git reset HEAD <file>`) or stash them (see Step 6c) before building your commit.

**Step 6b: Stage only your pathspecs, then ASSERT before committing**:
```bash
# Stage explicit files (yours only)
git add path/to/your/file1 path/to/your/file2

# Pre-commit ASSERTION: staged set must contain NONE of the known unrelated paths.
# Maintain a deny-pattern of paths that are NOT part of this change.
DENY='(^other-packet/|/install-guide|^docs/install/|UNRELATED_WIP)'
if git diff --cached --name-only | grep -E "$DENY"; then
  echo "ABORT: unrelated paths are staged — un-stage before committing"; 
else
  echo "OK: staged set is clean"
fi
```
Adjust `DENY` to the concrete unrelated paths you identified in Step 6a. A non-empty grep means STOP and re-stage; do not commit.

**Step 6c: If you must clear the tree first, use stash carefully**:
```bash
git stash push -k -m "unrelated WIP"   # -k/--keep-index keeps YOUR staged change, stashes the rest
# ... build and verify your commit ...
git stash pop
git diff --cached --name-only          # RE-CHECK: `git stash pop` can restore entries as STAGED
```
> **Caveat**: `git stash pop` can restore previously-staged entries back into the index as staged. Always re-run `git diff --cached --name-only` after a pop and re-assert against your deny-pattern before the next commit.

**Step 6d: Recovery if unrelated WIP already got committed**:
```bash
git reset --mixed HEAD~1               # Un-commit, KEEP all changes (staged → unstaged)
git status --short                     # Confirm nothing is staged
git add path/to/your/file1 path/to/your/file2   # Re-stage YOUR pathspecs only
git diff --cached --name-only | grep -E "$DENY"  # Re-assert: must be empty
git commit -m "type(scope): description" -m "Body explaining why"
```
`--mixed` (the default for `git reset`) un-commits and unstages while preserving file contents in the working tree, so unrelated WIP returns to its prior uncommitted state rather than being lost.

**Validation**: `scoped_staging_verified`

---

## 4. DECISION MATRIX

| Scenario | Strategy | Commit Type | Notes |
|----------|----------|-------------|-------|
| Single feature with tests | Single commit | `feat` | Tests belong with feature |
| Bug fix + unrelated refactor | Multiple commits | `fix`, `refactor` | Separate concerns |
| Documentation only | Single commit | `docs` | Unless multiple unrelated topics |
| Multiple independent fixes | Multiple commits | `fix` (each) | One fix per commit |
| Feature + breaking change | Single commit | `feat` | Note breaking change in footer |
| Internal artifacts present | Exclude artifacts | N/A | Don't commit, don't add to .gitignore |
| Test files in wrong location | Exclude from commit | N/A | Fix structure first |
| Config + code changes | Single commit (if related) | `feat` or `fix` | Or split if config is breaking change |

# Continuous Integration - Always-Current Live Branch

Keep the operator's IDE checkout continuously reflecting every concurrent AI session's committed work — while every session keeps its own isolated worktree and MCP databases.

---

## 1. OVERVIEW

### Purpose

The launch wrapper `worktree-session.sh` isolates every top-level session into its own worktree on a `work/<runtime>/<slug>` branch with isolated MCP databases. That isolation is what makes concurrent, multi-runtime work safe, but it also makes each session's work **invisible** in the operator's IDE, which is open on the primary checkout. Sharing one working tree across sessions is not an option: concurrent uncommitted writers on a single tree corrupt each other.

### When to Use

- When concurrent sessions need each session's committed work to reach the operator's primary checkout while each session keeps its isolated worktree and MCP databases.

### How It Works

The continuous-integration workflow resolves this by giving the operator one **live branch**, whatever branch the primary checkout is on, that always reflects every session's committed work within seconds:

- Sessions keep their isolated worktree (safe writes and DB isolation are unchanged).
- On each commit, the session **publishes** to the live branch through a safe primitive.
- The IDE checkout **fast-forward-follows** the live branch.

**Core principle**: isolate writes, integrate commits. Visibility is at commit granularity — the operator sees another session's work seconds after it commits, never its un-committed editor buffer. Real-time sub-commit sharing is deliberately out of scope: it would require a shared filesystem and reintroduce the concurrent-writer corruption this design avoids.

---

## 2. THE FOUR SCRIPTS

| Script | Role | Runs where |
|--------|------|-----------|
| `.skilled/bin/git-sync.sh` | Publish a session's commits to the live branch | Each session (via the `post-commit` hook, or manually) |
| `.skilled/bin/git-live-follow.sh` | Fast-forward the IDE checkout as the live branch advances | The operator's primary checkout |
| `.skilled/bin/git-primary-reconcile.sh` | Reconcile clean primary-checkout drift at SessionStart | The operator's primary checkout, backgrounded by each runtime |
| `.skilled/bin/worktree-status.sh` | Glance dashboard of every worktree's ahead / behind / dirty state | Anywhere (read-only) |

### `git-sync.sh` — the publish primitive

```
git-sync.sh [--live <branch>] [--remote <name>] [--auto] [--quiet]
```

It resolves the live branch (`--live`, else `$SPECKIT_LIVE_BRANCH`) and the remote (default `origin`), refuses to publish when the current branch *is* the live branch, then loops:


1. `git fetch` the live branch.
2. If HEAD is already contained in the live tip → nothing to publish.
3. If the live tip is an ancestor of HEAD → **fast-forward publish** (`git push origin HEAD:<live>`).
4. Otherwise the live branch moved → **rebase** the session's commits onto it, then publish. The rebase runs only when tracked files are clean, and only when no rebase is already in progress: a pre-existing `rebase-merge`/`rebase-apply` state directory (a stale or foreign rebase) is refused untouched, because aborting a rebase this hook did not start would rewind the branch to that rebase's orig-head and drop every commit made since. Untracked scratch files never block the rebase.
5. Any rebase conflict → `git rebase --abort`, then an assertion that HEAD returned to the exact pre-rebase commit — restored with `git reset --hard` if the abort moved it — and a printed manual-resolution path; the commit stays local and unpublished.

`--auto` (used by the hook) makes every exit code `0` so a blocked publish never fails the triggering commit. A push race retries the whole fetch→publish loop a bounded number of times.

### `git-live-follow.sh` — the IDE follower

```
git-live-follow.sh [--live <branch>] [--interval <sec>] [--once]
```

Polls the live branch and fast-forwards the checkout when the local tip is an ancestor of the remote tip, through git's own `--ff-only`. That primitive refuses to overwrite a modified tracked file, so a checkout carrying unrelated work-in-progress still follows for disjoint commits, while a commit that would touch a locally-edited file is reported and left for the operator — an in-progress edit in the IDE is never clobbered. A diverged branch is likewise reported, never overwritten. Run it once per IDE session (e.g. backgrounded), or `--once` for a manual "catch me up."

### `git-primary-reconcile.sh` - the SessionStart convergence step

Every runtime backgrounds the same script at SessionStart, so primary-checkout correctness does not depend on a long-running follower surviving between sessions. The script acts only when `git-dir` and `git-common-dir` resolve to the same path and the checkout is on the resolved live branch. Linked worktrees, detached HEADs, and intentional feature branches are zero-exit no-ops.

- A behind-only checkout fast-forwards through git's own `--ff-only`, which refuses to overwrite a modified tracked file, so a checkout carrying unrelated work-in-progress still follows for disjoint commits and is never clobbered on a collision. Untracked build output is intentionally ignored.
- Rebasing is the hard clean-tree boundary: because it rewrites commits across the working tree, unpublished local commits are rebased onto `origin/<live>` and published only when the tracked tree is clean; otherwise they are left preserved and unpublished.
- A pre-existing `rebase-merge`/`rebase-apply` state directory is refused untouched: the reconcile never aborts a rebase it did not start, so it cannot rewind the branch to a foreign orig-head and silently drop a just-made commit.
- A conflict aborts, then asserts HEAD returned to the exact pre-rebase commit, restoring it with `git reset --hard` if the abort moved it, and clean tracked state.
- A rejected push classifies the stable `[gate:<name>]` marker and leaves the local commit preserved but unpublished.

- The common-dir single-flight lock prevents concurrent SessionStarts from racing and treats a short-TTL stale lock as free.
- Fetch and push are time-bounded.
- Skips, advances, publications, and blocks append to `git-primary-reconcile.log`.
- Every internal outcome exits zero so SessionStart cannot be blocked.

### `worktree-status.sh` — the dashboard

```
worktree-status.sh [--live <branch>] [--fetch]
```

Read-only. Prints each worktree's branch, ahead / behind vs the live branch, and uncommitted file count. **Ahead + dirty is exactly the work not yet visible** in the IDE (ahead = committed-but-unpublished; dirty = uncommitted).

---

## 3. AUTOSYNC (COMMIT → PUBLISH)

Publishing is automatic. The versioned `post-commit` git hook calls `git-sync.sh --auto` after every commit, behind a tight triple gate so it fires **only** for a launch-wrapper session and **never** for the primary checkout or a manual commit:

1. `SPECKIT_AUTOSYNC=1` **and** `SPECKIT_LIVE_BRANCH` are present — the launch wrapper is the sole place that exports both.
2. The commit happened inside a **linked worktree** (`git rev-parse --absolute-git-dir` differs from the resolved `--git-common-dir`).
3. The call is fully non-fatal (`|| true`), and `post-commit`'s exit status is ignored by git regardless.

The launch wrapper wires this up per session: it resolves the live branch from the primary checkout, bases the new session worktree on it, and exports `SPECKIT_LIVE_BRANCH` + `SPECKIT_AUTOSYNC`. Orchestrated children inherit those env vars and correctly publish their own commits from inside the same worktree.

32: ## 2. OVERVIEW
33: 
34: ### Why This Skill Exists
35: 
36: A shared repository with many AI sessions fails quietly unless the git workflow has rules. Branch names drift, numbers collide, commits become unreproducible and cleanup stalls. sk-git exists to hold those rules so a fleet of sessions can share one repository without stepping on each other.
37: 
38: ### What It Does
39: 
40: sk-git runs the git workflow in three phases, from workspace setup through commit hygiene to completion.
41: 
42: - Setup creates an isolated worktree or keeps the current branch.
43: - Commit hygiene turns staged changes into deterministic Conventional Commit subjects with artifact filtering.
44: - Completion opens a PR, merges or discards, then cleans up.
45: - A smart router loads only the reference for the phase you are in, so the agent reads focused guidance instead of the whole library.
46: 
47: What makes sk-git different from raw git is the rule set it holds:
48: 
49: - Branch names carry their owner.
50: - Numbers come from a clone-wide allocator under a lock, never a hand-count.
51: - The skill asks before it touches your workspace.
52: - Commits are byte-for-byte reproducible from the same diff.
53: 
54: None of these are git defaults. Each rule exists to stop a specific quiet failure before it compounds.
55: 
56: ### What It Does Not Own
57: 
58: sk-git does not write code or manage spec folders. `sk-code` owns the code that gets committed. `system-spec-kit` owns spec folders with their memory and continuity layers. sk-git commits and integrates that work without claiming it.
59: 
60: ### The Git Workspace Safety Layer
61: 
62: | Feature | What the skill operates |
63: |---|---|
64: | **Numbered worktree grammar** | Worktree-backed branches use `worktrees/NNN-slug` with the directory `.worktrees/NNN-slug`. Dedicated branches without a worktree use `branches/NNN-slug` |
65: | **Per-namespace number allocator** | Reserves the next `NNN` under a lock per namespace (`worktrees/` and `branches/` each number independently), reading that namespace's high-water mark plus every matching worktree and ref |
66: | **Ask-first workspace rule** | Never picks worktree vs current branch on its own. Holds your choice for the session |
67: | **Launch-wrapper isolation** | An operator opt-in that places each top-level session in its own worktree and branch, with isolated MCP databases |
68: | **Continuous-integration autosync** | Publishes each commit to one shared live branch so the operator's IDE stays current |
69: | **Worktree reaper** | Auto-reaps qualifying wrapper worktrees and, with `--numbered`, finished numbered worktrees that are clean, merged, idle and hold nothing unrecoverable. Keeps and reports the rest, and signals no process other than the fsmonitor daemon of a worktree it removes |
70: | **Deterministic commits** | The same diff and metadata always produce the same Conventional Commit subject |
71: | **Safety refusals** | Blocks no-verify bypasses, secrets in a diff, amending published commits and force-pushing main |
72: | **Preflight advisory** | Evaluates every git command against 17 state-gated rules across all seven AI runtimes and prints the matching rule before it runs. Advisory only, never blocking (see `scripts/hooks/README.md`) |

92: 
93: # Or read the runtime instructions
94: Read(".skilled/skills/sk-git/SKILL.md")
95: ```
96: 
97: The advisor prints a routing recommendation. The Read call opens the runtime instructions.
98: 
99: **Step 2: Pick your phase.** New work starts at setup. Staged changes go to commit. Finished work goes to integration.
100: 
101: **Step 3: Confirm the workspace (setup only).** The skill asks before it creates anything. Choose an isolated worktree for parallel or long-running work. Stay on the current branch for a quick fix.
102: 
103: ```bash
104: # Numbered worktree: the allocator reserves a collision-free number under a
105: # per-namespace lock and creates the branch plus directory together.
106: bash .skilled/skills/sk-git/scripts/worktree-naming.sh create add-oauth-login
107: # -> branch worktrees/007-add-oauth-login, directory .worktrees/007-add-oauth-login
108:

110: bash .skilled/skills/sk-git/scripts/worktree-naming.sh create-branch external-dep

115:

118: ## 4. HOW IT WORKS
119: 
120: ### Numbered Worktree Grammar
121: 
122: Every managed name follows one grammar:
123: 
124: ```text
125: WORKTREE_BRANCH := "worktrees/" NNN "-" SLUG        (NNN 3-digit 001..999)
126: WORKTREE_DIR    := BASE "/" NNN "-" SLUG             (BASE default ".worktrees")
127: BASE            := ".worktrees" | <absolute path>    (override: speckit.worktreeBase)
128: DEDICATED_BRANCH:= "branches/" NNN "-" SLUG          (a branch with NO worktree)
129: RELEASE         := "skilled/v" A "." B "." C "." D

131: RESERVED        := "main"

133: ```

Deleting a middle number never back-fills the gap. `backup/<anything>` safety refs and the launch wrapper's `work/{runtime}/{slug}` lane stay distinct legal-but-not-numbered namespaces.

137: - `BASE` defaults to `.worktrees` inside the checkout. 143: 
144: - Git cannot enforce sequential uniqueness itself, so each namespace's counter is allocated under a lock in the shared common Git dir.

146: - Because the lock serializes contenders and the scan reads the high-water mark first, a partial scan can never reissue a live number, even when several sessions allocate at the same moment.
147: - Never hand-compute `NNN`. Call `worktree-naming.sh create`, `create-branch`, or `allocate` and let the lock do its job.
148:

150: 
151: ### Workspace Choice Is Always Yours
152: 
153: The skill never decides your branch strategy on its own. Every session that starts new work asks you to choose an isolated worktree or the current branch. The skill holds that choice for the rest of the session.
154: 
155: New branches are created one way only, through `git worktree add -b ...`. The direct commands never create branches:
156: 
157: - `git branch`
158: - `git checkout -b`
159: - `git switch -c`
160: 
161: A branch never exists without a worktree set up for it.
162: 
163: ### Launch Wrapper And Continuous Integration
164: 
165: The ask-first rule governs in-session decisions. It is separate from `.skilled/bin/worktree-session.sh`, a launch wrapper the operator opts into at the shell (for example `alias claude='bash /abs/.skilled/bin/worktree-session.sh claude'`). The wrapper runs before the AI starts and places each top-level session in its own worktree and branch, with isolated MCP databases. Orchestrated children exec in place. Because the operator aliased the launch, the choice was already made, so the wrapper does not violate the in-session rule.
166: 
167: Worktree isolation keeps concurrent sessions safe, but it also hides each session's work from the operator's IDE, which is open on the primary checkout. Continuous integration resolves that without giving up isolation. Each session autosyncs every commit to one shared live branch. The IDE fast-forward-follows it. Visibility is at commit granularity only, never another session's uncommitted buffer. The `post-commit` hook publishes through `git-sync.sh`. The script fetches and fast-forwards the shared branch or aborts on conflict. It pushes without force.
168: 
169: ### Deterministic Commit Messages
170: 
171: - The same diff and metadata always produce the same commit subject.
172: - Type inference takes the first match in a fixed priority order: release, docs, fix, feat, perf, refactor, test, ci, build then style.
173: - Scope inference maps file paths the same way, with the skill name taking priority over the agent or command directory, which beats the dominant top-level path.
174: - The history reads consistently no matter which session or model produced it.
175: - Every commit also ends with a contiguous trailer paragraph.
176: - Packet work carries `Spec: <track>/<packet>[/<phase>...]`, and every commit carries `Commit-Id: NNNNNNN`, a seven-digit repository-wide ordinal minted once under a lock.
177: - An amend keeps the id the commit already owns unless `-m` replaces the message, while a cherry-pick drops the copied id and mints a fresh one.
178: - The stamper fails open: when the allocator cannot answer, the commit lands unstamped and the commit-msg hook still validates what is there.
179: - Three queries read the trailer back with no extra tooling:
180:   - `git log -E --grep='^Spec: your-track/your-packet'` lists a packet's commits
181:   - `git log --fixed-strings --grep='Commit-Id: 0009113'` finds the commit that owns an ordinal
182:   - `git log --format='%(trailers:key=Commit-Id,valueonly)'` lists every stamped id
183: 
184: ### Cleanup And Safety Refusals
185: 
186: Finishing is not done when the PR merges. The completion flow removes the worktree directory and deletes the local feature branch. It drops the remote tracking branch too, so branches and worktrees do not accumulate. A test gate blocks the merge or PR while tests fail.
187: 
188: The skill also refuses a fixed set of unsafe actions: a `--no-verify` bypass, a diff carrying secrets, amending a published commit and a force push to `main`. The script fetches and fast-forwards the shared branch or aborts on conflict. It pushes without force.
168: 
169: ### Deterministic Commit Messages
170: 
171: - The same diff and metadata always produce the same commit subject.
172: - Type inference takes the first match in a fixed priority order: release, docs, fix, feat, perf, refactor, test, ci, build then style.
173: - Scope inference maps file paths the same way, with the skill name taking priority over the agent or command directory, which beats the dominant top-level path.
174: - The history reads consistently no matter which session or model produced it.
175: - Every commit also ends with a contiguous trailer paragraph.
176: - Packet work carries `Spec: <track>/<packet>[/<phase>...]`, and every commit carries `Commit-Id: NNNNNNN`, a seven-digit repository-wide ordinal minted once under a lock.
177: - An amend keeps the id the commit already owns unless `-m` replaces the message, while a cherry-pick drops the copied id and mints a fresh one.
178: - The stamper fails open: when the allocator cannot answer, the commit lands unstamped and the commit-msg hook still validates what is there.
179: - Three queries read the trailer back with no extra tooling:
180:   - `git log -E --grep='^Spec: your-track/your-packet'` lists a packet's commits
181:   - `git log --fixed-strings --grep='Commit-Id: 0009113'` finds the commit that owns an ordinal
182:   - `git log --format='%(trailers:key=Commit-Id,valueonly)'` lists every stamped id
183: 
184: ### Cleanup And Safety Refusals
185: 
186: Finishing is not done when the PR merges. The completion flow removes the worktree directory and deletes the local feature branch. It drops the remote tracking branch too, so branches and worktrees do not accumulate. A test gate blocks the merge or PR while tests fail.
187: 
188: The skill also refuses a fixed set of unsafe actions: a `--no-verify` bypass, a diff carrying secrets, amending a published commit and a force push to `main`. It never stashes or rebases a primary tree that is dirty or diverged. It also never resets a tree owned by a concurrent session, because forcing a sync there can orphan that session's work.

252: ## 6. TROUBLESHOOTING
253: 
254: | What you see | Why | Fix |
255: |---|---|---|
256: | Merge conflicts the AI will not resolve | Overlapping edits need a human call on which version wins | Escalate. The skill does not auto-resolve semantic conflicts |

265: ## 7. FAQ
266: 
267: **Q: Why does it always ask before creating a branch?**
268: 
269: A: Workspace strategy has real consequences. An unnecessary worktree adds overhead. Staying in place when parallel work is planned causes conflicts. Context alone does not say which is right, so the skill asks every time.
270: 
271: **Q: Why can I not use `git checkout -b` or `git switch -c`?**
272: 
273: A: Those create a branch with no worktree isolation. sk-git keeps branch creation and workspace setup atomic through `git worktree add -b ...`. For an in-place branch, choose the current-branch option and skip setup.
274: 
275: **Q: Why an allocator instead of just picking the next free number?**
276: 
277: A: Several sessions allocate at once. Picking a number by eye races: two sessions read the same maximum and both reserve it. The allocator takes a clone-wide lock and seeds from the high-water mark plus every worktree and ref, so a live number is never reissued.
278: 
279: **Q: When do I use the `gh` CLI versus the GitHub MCP?**
280: 
281: A: Use `gh` for simple PR creation and listing. Use the GitHub MCP when you need structured data back, such as PR reviews and issue fields, plus CI run details. It also handles bulk operations across many PRs or issues.
282: 
283: **Q: A PR merged but the worktree was never cleaned up. Now what?**
284: 
285: A: Run `git worktree list` to find the stale one, remove it with `git worktree remove .worktrees/{NNN}-{slug}`, delete the local branch with `git branch -d worktrees/{NNN}-{slug}` (or `branches/{NNN}-{slug}`) and the remote with `git push origin --delete worktrees/{NNN}-{slug}`, then `git worktree prune`. Remove the worktree before deleting its branch, because a branch checked out by a worktree cannot be deleted.
286: 
287: **Q: How do I find the commits for a packet?**
288: 
289: A: Grep the `Spec:` trailer with the packet query: `git log -E --grep='^Spec: your-track/your-packet'`. Substitute the track and packet you want. Every matching commit names that packet in its trailer paragraph, so the result needs no other index.

### Step 4: Create Worktree

**Purpose**: Create the isolated workspace under the numbered-worktree `worktrees/{NNN}-{slug}` grammar

#### Naming Convention

Named feature worktrees — the ones a human creates for a feature or a parallel task —
use one unified, numbered grammar:

- **Branch**: `worktrees/{NNN}-{slug}` — e.g. `worktrees/001-add-oauth`. A dedicated
  branch with no worktree uses `branches/{NNN}-{slug}` — e.g.
  `branches/002-external-dep`. Flat spec-style namespaces keep the Git-UI branch
  tree legible as a few clean folders instead of a per-skill pile. `{slug}` is a
  short kebab description.
- **Directory**: `<repo-root>/.worktrees/{NNN}-{slug}` — e.g.
  `.worktrees/001-add-oauth`. `.worktrees/` is the repo-local,
  already-gitignored worktree home. The directory mirrors the branch tail exactly.
- **`{NNN}`** is a 3-digit zero-padded **per-namespace** counter (001..999).
  `worktrees/` and `branches/` each number independently, strictly sequential,
  never skipped or reused: a `worktrees/003` and a `branches/003` may coexist,
  and deleting a middle number never back-fills the gap (next = max-in-use + 1).
  Git cannot enforce sequential uniqueness itself, so the counter is allocated by
  `.skilled/skills/sk-git/scripts/worktree-naming.sh`, which:
  - holds a lock in the shared common git dir;
  - seeds each namespace's max from its stored high-water mark, every matching
    local + remote ref, and (for `worktrees/`) every registered worktree basename;

The lock serializes contenders, and the scan reads the high-water mark first, so a partial scan can never reissue a live number. Never hand-compute `{NNN}`.

> **Two distinct lanes.** This `worktrees/{NNN}-{slug}` grammar is for *named feature
> worktrees a human creates*. It is separate from the per-session **ephemeral**
> worktrees allocated by the launch wrapper `.skilled/bin/worktree-session.sh`, which
> keep their own auto-managed namespace — branch `work/{runtime}/{slug}`, directory
> `.worktrees/{runtime}-{slug}` — and are auto-reaped by `worktree-reaper.sh` (which keys
> on the branch prefix `work/`, and only when the wrapper worktree is clean, merged into
> the live integration tip, and proven inactive by its session marker). Those ephemeral
> session worktrees are intentionally **not** numbered; do not assign them an `{NNN}`.
> `backup/<anything>` safety refs are likewise legal but not numbered task branches.

The GitKraken MCP server (`@gitkraken/gk`) exposes local git operations, GitLens AI workflows, and cross-platform issue/PR management across GitHub, GitLab, Azure DevOps, Bitbucket, and Jira.

### When to Use

193: - Core Principle, Boundaries and Key Sources follow Purpose and When to Use, in that order, and each appears only when it has content.

195: - Rule fields are `- **Label:** text` bullets, never two bold labels on consecutive lines.
196: - Links are `[title](url)`, never a bare URL.
197: - Every `---` has a blank line above it, so a divider never turns the line above into a setext heading.
198: - A related section, when present, is the last H2.
199:

202: ### What Are AI Agent Skill Reference Files?
203: 
204: Reference files are detailed technical documentation in the `references/` directory that provide deep-dive guidance with **explicit reasoning** - making thought processes visible, showing decision logic, and analyzing root causes.
205: 
206: **Core Purpose**:
207: - **Technical depth** - Step-by-step reasoning with rationale
208: - **Phased workflows** - Structured processes with validation checkpoints
209: - **Pattern libraries** - Before/after examples, comparison tables
210: - **Tool integration** - MCP tools, scripts, asset references
211: - **Root cause analysis** - Systematic debugging and troubleshooting
212: 
213: **Key Difference from Generic Documentation**:
214: - AI agent skills = Actionable workflows with explicit reasoning
215: - Generic docs = Information reference without decision logic
216: 
217: ### Progressive Disclosure in Skills
218: 
219: ```
220: Level 1: Metadata (name + description)
221:          └─ Always in context (~100 words)
222:             ↓
223: Level 2: SKILL.md body
224:          └─ When skill triggers (<5k words)
225:             ↓
226: Level 3: Reference files (this document)
227:          └─ Loaded as needed (500-3000 lines per file)
228: ```
229: 
230: **Reference files = Level 3**: Deep technical guidance loaded only when the agent needs specific workflow details.

682: ## 5. CONVERTING LOGIC TO EXECUTABLE CODE
683: 
684: ### When to Extract Logic from Markdown
685: 
686: **Purpose**: Separate documentation from executable code for better maintainability, testability, and reusability.
687: 
688: **Decision Criteria**:
689: 
690: | Pattern Type          | Keep in Markdown  | Extract to Code           | Reasoning                                    |
691: | --------------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
692: | **Python functions**  | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/scripts/*.py`   | Type safety, unit testing, reusability       |
693: | **YAML configs**      | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/assets/*.yaml`  | Dynamic loading, version control, validation |
694: | **Decision trees**    | ⚠️ High-level only | ✅ Details → YAML + Python | Machine-readable, can be validated           |
695: | **Command mappings**  | ⚠️ Examples only   | ✅ Full map → YAML         | Easier maintenance, can be imported          |
696: | **Workflow diagrams** | ✅ Yes (generated) | ✅ Source → YAML           | YAML = source of truth, diagram = output     |
697: | **Checklists**        | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Human-readable is primary use case           |
698: | **Before/after code** | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Educational, not executable                  |
699: 
700: ### Extraction Pattern
701: 
702: **In Markdown (Reference File)**:
703: ```markdown
704: ### [Workflow Name]
705: 
706: [High-level description of what the workflow does]
707: 
708: **Implementation:** See [workflow_name.py](../scripts/workflow_name.py) for execution logic and [workflow-config.yaml](../assets/workflow-config.yaml) for configuration.
709: 
710: **Quick Overview**:
711: 1. [Step 1 - high level]
712: 2. [Step 2 - high level]
713: 3. [Step 3 - high level]
714: 
715: **Configuration Options:**
716: - See YAML config for customizable parameters
717: - Default values optimized for common use cases
718: ```
719: 
720: ### Benefits of Separation
721: 
722: - **Type safety** - Python type hints catch errors at development time
723: - **Testability** - Unit tests for logic, integration tests for workflows
724: - **Reusability** - Imported by multiple skills or scripts
725: - **Version control** - Git diffs show logic changes clearly
726: - **Schema validation** - YAML can be validated against schemas
727: - **Dynamic loading** - Configuration changes without code edits
728: 
729: ### Example: Mode Detection Extraction
730: 
731: **❌ BEFORE** (inline Python in markdown):
732: \```python
733: def detect_mode(request):
734:     if '$quick' in request: return 'quick', 5
735:     elif '$ticket' in request: return 'ticket', 10
736:     return 'interactive', 10
737: \```
738: 
739: **✅ AFTER** (extracted with type safety):
740: 
741: `/scripts/mode_detection.py`:
742: \```python
743: from dataclasses import dataclass
744: 
745: @dataclass
746: class ModeConfig:
747:     mode: str
748:     depth_rounds: int
749: 
750: def detect_mode(request: str) -> ModeConfig:
751:     """Detect mode from command shortcuts."""
752:     if '$quick' in request:
753:         return ModeConfig('quick', 5)
754:     elif '$ticket' in request:
755:         return ModeConfig('ticket', 10)
756:     return ModeConfig('interactive', 10)
757: \```
758: 
759: `/tests/test_mode_detection.py`:
760: \```python
761: def test_quick_mode():
762:     assert detect_mode("$quick fix").mode == 'quick'
763: \```
764: 
765: **Why better:** Type hints, testable, reusable, separated from docs
766:

769: ## 6. YAML CONFIGURATION PATTERNS
770: 
771: ### Purpose
772: 
773: **YAML for configuration data** - Separate configuration from documentation for easier maintenance and dynamic loading.
774: 
775: **When to use YAML**:
776: - Configuration data (thresholds, mappings, rules)
777: - Data structures (nested objects, lists)
778: - Workflow definitions (step sequences, pipelines)
779: - Decision trees (conditional logic patterns)
780: - Validation schemas
781: 
782: ### Standard YAML Structure
783: 
784: ```yaml
785: # [config-name].yaml
786: metadata:
787:   version: "1.0.0"
788:   description: "Configuration for [feature name]"
789: 
790: config:
791:   threshold_values:
792:     low: 1
793:     medium: 5
794:     high: 10
795:   feature_flags:
796:     enable_feature_x: true
797:   mappings:
798:     $quick: "quick_mode"
799:     $ticket: "ticket_mode"
800: ```
801: 
802: ### File Organization
803: 
804: ```
805: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
806: ├── assets/
807: │   ├── workflow-configs/
808: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
809: │   │   ├── variant-detection.yaml
810: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
811: │   ├── mappings/
812: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
813: │   │   ├── mode-recognition.yaml
814: │   │   └── shortcut-definitions.yaml
815: │   └── templates/
816: │       └── [template files]
817: ```
818: 
819: ### Loading Pattern (Python)
820: 
821: ```python
822: import yaml
823: from pathlib import Path
824: 
825: def load_config(config_name: str) -> dict:
826:     """Load YAML config from assets directory."""
827:     config_path = Path(__file__).parent.parent / f"assets/{config_name}.yaml"
828:     with open(config_path) as f:
829:         return yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
830: 
831: # Usage
832: config = load_config("canvas-methodology")
833: ```
834: 
835: ### Example: Variant Detection Rules
836: 
837: **❌ BEFORE** (markdown table):
838: ```markdown
839: | Trigger                    | Action             |
840: | -------------------------- | ------------------ |
841: | "show options"             | Offer 3-5 variants |
842: | Complexity 7+ + "not sure" | Offer variants     |
843: ```
844: 
845: **✅ AFTER** (YAML + Python):
846: 
847: `/assets/variant-detection-rules.yaml`:
848: ```yaml
849: config:
850:   variant_triggers:
851:     explicit_keywords: ["show me options", "variations"]
852:     implicit:
853:       complexity_threshold: 7
854:       uncertainty_signals: ["not sure", "what would work"]
855:   variant_count:
856:     simple: [2, 3]
857:     complex: [5, 10]
858: ```
859: 
860: `/scripts/variant_detector.py`:
861: ```python
862: import yaml
863: 
864: class VariantDetector:
865:     def __init__(self, config_path: str):
866:         with open(config_path) as f:
867:             self.config = yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
868: 
869:     def should_generate_variants(self, request: str, complexity: int) -> bool:
870:         keywords = self.config['variant_triggers']['explicit_keywords']
871:         if any(kw in request.lower() for kw in keywords):
872:             return True
873: 
874:         threshold = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['complexity_threshold']
875:         if complexity >= threshold:
876:             signals = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['uncertainty_signals']
877:             return any(s in request.lower() for s in signals)
878:         return False
879: ```
880: 
881: **Why better:** Dynamic config loading, easier maintenance, schema validation possible
882:

885: ## 7. PYTHON SCRIPT INTEGRATION
886: 
887: ### When to Use Python for Logic
888: 
889: **Use Python scripts when**:
890: - Procedural logic (workflows, algorithms)
891: - Complex conditionals (multi-step decisions)
892: - Data transformation (processing, validation)
893: - API integration (external services)
894: - File operations (reading, parsing, generating)
895: 
896: ### Type Hints and Docstring Standards
897: 
898: **Always include**:
899: - Type hints for parameters and return values
900: - Google-style docstrings (Args, Returns, Raises, Examples)
901: - Dataclasses for structured data
902: 
903: **Example**:
904: ```python
905: from dataclasses import dataclass
906: from pathlib import Path
907: 
908: @dataclass
909: class ValidationResult:
910:     is_valid: bool
911:     errors: list[str]
912: 
913: def validate_config(config_path: Path) -> ValidationResult:
914:     """
915:     Validate configuration file.
916: 
917:     Args:
918:         config_path: Path to YAML config file
919: 
920:     Returns:
921:         ValidationResult with status and errors
922: 
923:     Raises:
924:         FileNotFoundError: If config doesn't exist
925:     """
926:     if not config_path.exists():
927:         raise FileNotFoundError(f"Config not found: {config_path}")
928:     # Validation logic
929:     return ValidationResult(is_valid=True, errors=[])
930: ```
931: 
932: ### Unit Testing Requirements
933: 
934: **Every Python script must have tests**:
935: - Naming: `test_[script_name].py` in `/tests/` directory
936: - Coverage: ≥80% line coverage
937: - Framework: pytest
938: 
939: **Example**:
940: ```python
941: import pytest
942: from scripts.config_validator import validate_config
943: 
944: def test_validate_success(tmp_path):
945:     config = tmp_path / "config.yaml"
946:     config.write_text("config:\n  threshold: 5")
947:     result = validate_config(config)
948:     assert result.is_valid
949: 
950: def test_validate_missing_file():
951:     with pytest.raises(FileNotFoundError):
952:         validate_config(Path("nonexistent.yaml"))
953: ```
954: 
955: ### Import and Reference Patterns
956: 
957: **Python import order**: Standard library → Third-party → Local
958: 
959: **Markdown references**:
960: ```markdown
961: **See also:** [script_name.py](../scripts/script_name.py), [config.yaml](../assets/config.yaml)
962: ```
963: 
964: ### Example: Workflow Decision Logic
965: 
966: **❌ BEFORE** (text decision tree):
967: ```markdown
968: IF "$quick": use quick mode (5 rounds)
969: IF "$ticket": use ticket mode (10 rounds)
970: OTHERWISE: use interactive mode
971: ```
972: 
973: **✅ AFTER** (Python with type safety):
974: 
975: `/scripts/workflow_router.py`:
976: ```python
977: from typing import Literal
978: from dataclasses import dataclass
979: 
980: WorkflowMode = Literal["quick", "ticket", "interactive"]
981: 
982: @dataclass
983: class WorkflowDecision:
984:     mode: WorkflowMode
985:     depth_rounds: int
986: 
987: def route_workflow(request: str) -> WorkflowDecision:
988:     """Route request to appropriate workflow."""
989:     if '$quick' in request.lower():
990:         return WorkflowDecision("quick", 5)
991:     if '$ticket' in request.lower():
992:         return WorkflowDecision("ticket", 10)
993:     return WorkflowDecision("interactive", 10)
994: ```
995: 
996: `/tests/test_workflow_router.py`:
997: ```python
998: def test_quick_mode():
999:     assert route_workflow("$quick fix").mode == "quick"
1000: 
1001: def test_default_mode():
1002:     assert route_workflow("help me").mode == "interactive"
1003: ```
1004: 
1005: **Why better:** Type-safe with Literal, testable, structured with dataclass
1006: 
1007: ---
1008: 
1009: ## 8. STANDARD STRUCTURE TEMPLATE
1010: 
1011: ### Complete Skill Directory Structure
1012: 
1013: **Path:** `.skilled/skills/` (singular, not `skills` or `openskills`)
1014: 
1015: ```
1016: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
1017: ├── SKILL.md                    # Main skill file (Level 2 in progressive disclosure)
1018: ├── references/                 # Deep-dive technical documentation (Level 3)
1019: │   ├── workflow-name.md        # Multi-phase workflows with checkpoints (kebab-case)
1020: │   ├── patterns-library.md     # Before/after code patterns (kebab-case)
1021: │   ├── debugging-guide.md      # Systematic troubleshooting (kebab-case)
1022: │   └── quick-reference.md      # Commands, shortcuts, checklists (kebab-case)
1023: ├── scripts/                    # Executable Python logic
1024: │   ├── mode_detection.py       # Procedural logic, algorithms
1025: │   ├── workflow_router.py      # Decision logic
1026: │   ├── config_validator.py     # Data transformation
1027: │   └── __init__.py             # Package initialization
1028: ├── assets/                     # Configuration and data files
1029: │   ├── workflow-configs/       # YAML workflow definitions
1030: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
1031: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
1032: │   ├── mappings/               # YAML mapping data
1033: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
1034: │   │   └── mode-recognition.yaml
1035: │   └── templates/              # Markdown/code templates
1036: │       ├── template-name.md
1037: │       └── component-template.tsx
1038: └── tests/                      # Unit and integration tests
1039:     ├── test_mode_detection.py
1040:     ├── test_workflow_router.py
1041:     ├── test_config_validator.py
1042:     └── __init__.py
1043: ```
1044: 
1045: ### Directory Purposes
1046: 
1047: **SKILL.md** (Required): Overview, workflow (3-5 steps), rules. Target: <200 lines
1048: 
1049: **references/** (Optional): Detailed workflows, patterns, debugging. Target: 500-3000 lines/file. **All authored filenames must use kebab-case.**
1050: 
1051: **scripts/** (Optional): Python logic - procedural, routing, validation. Requires type hints, tests
1052: 
1053: **assets/** (Optional): YAML configs, workflow definitions, templates, mappings
1054: 
1055: **tests/** (Required if scripts/ exists): Unit tests with ≥80% coverage, pytest, `test_[name].py`
1056: 
1057: ### When to Create Each Directory
1058: 
1059: | Directory     | Create When                                                     | Don't Create When                           |
1060: | ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
1061: | `references/` | Content >200 lines, multi-phase workflows, systematic debugging | Simple skills <200 lines total              |
1062: | `scripts/`    | Python logic extracted from markdown, reusable functions        | Pure documentation, no executable logic     |
1063: | `assets/`     | YAML configs, templates, structured data                        | No configuration data, inline examples only |
1064: | `tests/`      | `scripts/` directory exists                                     | No Python scripts to test                   |
1065: 
1066: ### Integration Pattern
1067: 
1068: **How components work together:**
1069: - SKILL.md references scripts: `[workflow_router.py](./scripts/workflow_router.py)`
1070: - Scripts load configs: `yaml.safe_load(f"../assets/config.yaml")`
1071: - Tests verify scripts: `assert route_workflow("input").mode == "expected"`
1072: - Markdown links to all: "See [script.py](../scripts/), [config.yaml](../assets/)"
1073:

14: # Skill Reference File Templates - AI Agent Skills
15: 
16: Templates for creating reference files in AI agent skills with deep-dive technical guidance.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Location & Naming
23: 
24: **Location:** `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/references/`
25: 
26: **Naming Convention:** kebab-case with `.md` extension only
27: 
28: | ✅ Valid Names | ❌ Invalid Names |
29: |---------------|-----------------|
30: | `implementation-workflows.md` | `ImplementationWorkflows.md` (PascalCase) |
31: | `tool-catalog.md` | `tool_catalog.md` (snake_case) |
32: | `debugging-guide.md` | `DebuggingGuide.MD` (wrong case) |
33: | `quick-reference.md` | `quickReference.md` (camelCase) |
34: | `code-quality-standards.md` | `code quality standards.md` (spaces) |
35: 
36: ---
37: 
38: ## 2. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
39: 
40: ### Document Structure: Title and Intro
41: 
42: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
43: 
44: ```markdown
45: ---
46: title: [Title]
47: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
48: trigger_phrases:
49:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
50:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
51:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
52: importance_tier: normal
53: contextType: general
54: version: 1.0.0.0
55: ---
56: 
57: # [Title]
58: 
59: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
60: 
61: ---
62: 
63: \## 1. OVERVIEW
64: [All detailed content goes here, NOT in the intro]
65: 
66: ```
67: 
68: Every reference file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content. `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, with `important` only for formal contract docs. `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.
69: 
70: > **WARNING: DO NOT duplicate content between intro and Section 1.**
71: > The intro is a hook. Section 1 provides the details.
72: 
73: #### GOOD Intro Structure
74: 
75: ```markdown
76: # Git Commit Workflows
77: 
78: This reference turns a mixed working tree into a small set of reviewable commits.
79: 
80: ---
81: 
82: \## 1. OVERVIEW
83: 
84: ### Purpose
85: Each rule keeps one commit focused on one intent, so history stays easy to read, review and revert.
86: 
87: ### When to Use
88: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
89: - Filtering generated files from commits
90: - Writing clear commit messages
91: 
92: ### Core Principle
93: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
94: ```
95: 
96: #### BAD Intro Structure (duplicates content)
97: 
98: ```markdown
99: # Git Commit Workflows
100: 
101: Step-by-step workflows for creating clean, atomic commits with proper filtering.
102: 
103: ### Core Principle   ← WRONG: No headers in intro!
104: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
105: 
106: ### When to Use      ← WRONG: This belongs in Section 1!
107: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
108: 
109: ---
110: 
111: \## 1. OVERVIEW
112: 
113: ### Purpose
114: Provides systematic workflows...  ← Now this duplicates the intro!
115: 
116: ### Core Principle
117: Atomic commits...  ← DUPLICATED from intro!
118: ```
119: 
120: #### Intro vs Section 1 Content Placement
121: 
122: | Content Type          | Intro (after H1) | Section 1 OVERVIEW |
123: | --------------------- | ---------------- | ------------------ |
124: | 1-2 sentence summary  | ✅ YES            | ❌ NO (don't repeat) |
125: | Core Principle        | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
126: | When to Use           | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
127: | Primary Sources       | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (as "Key Sources") |
128: | Purpose (detailed)    | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
129: | Prerequisites         | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
130: | Any H3 subsections    | ❌ NEVER          | ✅ YES              |
131: 
132: ---

134: ### Reference Body Skeleton
135: 
136: **Every reference body follows this order.** The hook and the Purpose say different things: the hook names the job, and the Purpose names the outcome.
137: 
138: ```markdown
139: # [Title]
140: 
141: [1-2 sentence hook: what this reference covers and when to reach for it.]
142: 
143: ---
144: 
145: ## 1. OVERVIEW
146: 
147: ### Purpose
148: 
149: [The outcome this reference produces, in one or two sentences.]
150: 
151: ### When to Use
152: 
153: - [Trigger that sends a reader here]
154: - [Second trigger]
155: 
156: ### Core Principle
157: 
158: [One-line statement that governs every rule below.]
159: 
160: ### Boundaries
161: 
162: - **In scope**: [What this reference owns]
163: - **Out of scope**: [What belongs in a sibling reference]
164: 
165: ### Key Sources
166: 
167: - [title](url) - [What the source establishes]
168: 
169: ---
170: 
171: ## 2. [CONTENT SECTION]
172: 
173: ### [Rule Group]
174: 
175: - **Rule:** [What to do]
176: - **Why:** [The failure it prevents]
177: - **Check:** [How to verify it]
178: 
179: ---
180: 
181: ## 3. [CONTENT SECTION]
182: 
183: [Body of the section]
184: 
185: ---
186: 
187: ## 4. RELATED RESOURCES
188: 
189: - [title](./sibling-reference.md) - [What the reader gets there]
190: ```
191: 
192: **Rules the skeleton encodes:**
193: - Core Principle, Boundaries and Key Sources follow Purpose and When to Use, in that order, and each appears only when it has content.
194: - Content sections use integer numbers only: `## 2.`, `## 3.`, and so on.
195: - Rule fields are `- **Label:** text` bullets, never two bold labels on consecutive lines.
196: - Links are `[title](url)`, never a bare URL.
197: - Every `---` has a blank line above it, so a divider never turns the line above into a setext heading.
198: - A related section, when present, is the last H2.

202: ### What Are AI Agent Skill Reference Files?
203: 
204: Reference files are detailed technical documentation in the `references/` directory that provide deep-dive guidance with **explicit reasoning** - making thought processes visible, showing decision logic, and analyzing root causes.
205: 
206: **Core Purpose**:
207: - **Technical depth** - Step-by-step reasoning with rationale
208: - **Phased workflows** - Structured processes with validation checkpoints
209: - **Pattern libraries** - Before/after examples, comparison tables
210: - **Tool integration** - MCP tools, scripts, asset references
211: - **Root cause analysis** - Systematic debugging and troubleshooting
212: 
213: **Key Difference from Generic Documentation**:
214: - AI agent skills = Actionable workflows with explicit reasoning
215: - Generic docs = Information reference without decision logic
216: 
217: ### Progressive Disclosure in Skills
218: 
219: ```
220: Level 1: Metadata (name + description)
221:          └─ Always in context (~100 words)
222:             ↓
223: Level 2: SKILL.md body
224:          └─ When skill triggers (<5k words)
225:             ↓
226: Level 3: Reference files (this document)
227:          └─ Loaded as needed (500-3000 lines per file)
228: ```

281: ## 4. AI AGENT SKILL REFERENCE CHARACTERISTICS

283: ### Core Principle Statements

285: **Purpose**: Distill philosophy into one-line wisdom

294:

308: - "ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure"

311: ### Phased Workflows with Validation

584: ### Phased Workflow with Checkpoints Example

586: **Purpose**: Show complete workflow with validation gates

681: 
682: ## 5. CONVERTING LOGIC TO EXECUTABLE CODE
683: 
684: ### When to Extract Logic from Markdown
685: 
686: **Purpose**: Separate documentation from executable code for better maintainability, testability, and reusability.
687: 
688: **Decision Criteria**:
689: 
690: | Pattern Type          | Keep in Markdown  | Extract to Code           | Reasoning                                    |
691: | --------------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
692: | **Python functions**  | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/scripts/*.py`   | Type safety, unit testing, reusability       |
693: | **YAML configs**      | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/assets/*.yaml`  | Dynamic loading, version control, validation |
694: | **Decision trees**    | ⚠️ High-level only | ✅ Details → YAML + Python | Machine-readable, can be validated           |
695: | **Command mappings**  | ⚠️ Examples only   | ✅ Full map → YAML         | Easier maintenance, can be imported          |
696: | **Workflow diagrams** | ✅ Yes (generated) | ✅ Source → YAML           | YAML = source of truth, diagram = output     |
697: | **Checklists**        | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Human-readable is primary use case           |
698: | **Before/after code** | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Educational, not executable                  |
699: 
700: ### Extraction Pattern
701: 
702: **In Markdown (Reference File)**:
703: ```markdown
704: ### [Workflow Name]
705: 
706: [High-level description of what the workflow does]
707: 
708: **Implementation:** See [workflow_name.py](../scripts/workflow_name.py) for execution logic and [workflow-config.yaml](../assets/workflow-config.yaml) for configuration.
709: 
710: **Quick Overview**:
711: 1. [Step 1 - high level]
712: 2. [Step 2 - high level]
713: 3. [Step 3 - high level]
714: 
715: **Configuration Options:**
716: - See YAML config for customizable parameters
717: - Default values optimized for common use cases
718: ```
719: 
720: ### Benefits of Separation
721: 
722: - **Type safety** - Python type hints catch errors at development time
723: - **Testability** - Unit tests for logic, integration tests for workflows
724: - **Reusability** - Imported by multiple skills or scripts
725: - **Version control** - Git diffs show logic changes clearly
726: - **Schema validation** - YAML can be validated against schemas
727: - **Dynamic loading** - Configuration changes without code edits
728: 
729: ### Example: Mode Detection Extraction
730: 
731: **❌ BEFORE** (inline Python in markdown):
732: \```python
733: def detect_mode(request):
734:     if '$quick' in request: return 'quick', 5
735:     elif '$ticket' in request: return 'ticket', 10
736:     return 'interactive', 10
737: \```
738: 
739: **✅ AFTER** (extracted with type safety):
740: 
741: `/scripts/mode_detection.py`:
742: \```python
743: from dataclasses import dataclass
744: 
745: @dataclass
746: class ModeConfig:
747:     mode: str
748:     depth_rounds: int
749: 
750: def detect_mode(request: str) -> ModeConfig:
751:     """Detect mode from command shortcuts."""
752:     if '$quick' in request:
753:         return ModeConfig('quick', 5)
754:     elif '$ticket' in request:
755:         return ModeConfig('ticket', 10)
756:     return ModeConfig('interactive', 10)
757: \```
758: 
759: `/tests/test_mode_detection.py`:
760: \```python
761: def test_quick_mode():
762:     assert detect_mode("$quick fix").mode == 'quick'
763: \```
764: 
765: **Why better:** Type hints, testable, reusable, separated from docs
766: 
767: ---
768: 
769: ## 6. YAML CONFIGURATION PATTERNS
770: 
771: ### Purpose
772: 
773: **YAML for configuration data** - Separate configuration from documentation for easier maintenance and dynamic loading.
774: 
775: **When to use YAML**:
776: - Configuration data (thresholds, mappings, rules)
777: - Data structures (nested objects, lists)
778: - Workflow definitions (step sequences, pipelines)
779: - Decision trees (conditional logic patterns)
780: - Validation schemas
781: 
782: ### Standard YAML Structure
783: 
784: ```yaml
785: # [config-name].yaml
786: metadata:
787:   version: "1.0.0"
788:   description: "Configuration for [feature name]"
789: 
790: config:
791:   threshold_values:
792:     low: 1
793:     medium: 5
794:     high: 10
795:   feature_flags:
796:     enable_feature_x: true
797:   mappings:
798:     $quick: "quick_mode"
799:     $ticket: "ticket_mode"
800: ```
801: 
802: ### File Organization
803: 
804: ```
805: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
806: ├── assets/
807: │   ├── workflow-configs/
808: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
809: │   │   ├── variant-detection.yaml
810: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
811: │   ├── mappings/
812: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
813: │   │   ├── mode-recognition.yaml
814: │   │   └── shortcut-definitions.yaml
815: │   └── templates/
816: │       └── [template files]
817: ```
818: 
819: ### Loading Pattern (Python)
820: 
821: ```python
822: import yaml
823: from pathlib import Path
824: 
825: def load_config(config_name: str) -> dict:
826:     """Load YAML config from assets directory."""
827:     config_path = Path(__file__).parent.parent / f"assets/{config_name}.yaml"
828:     with open(config_path) as f:
829:         return yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
830: 
831: # Usage
832: config = load_config("canvas-methodology")
833: ```
834: 
835: ### Example: Variant Detection Rules
836: 
837: **❌ BEFORE** (markdown table):
838: ```markdown
839: | Trigger                    | Action             |
840: | -------------------------- | ------------------ |
841: | "show options"             | Offer 3-5 variants |
842: | Complexity 7+ + "not sure" | Offer variants     |
843: ```
844: 
845: **✅ AFTER** (YAML + Python):
846: 
847: `/assets/variant-detection-rules.yaml`:
848: ```yaml
849: config:
850:   variant_triggers:
851:     explicit_keywords: ["show me options", "variations"]
852:     implicit:
853:       complexity_threshold: 7
854:       uncertainty_signals: ["not sure", "what would work"]
855:   variant_count:
856:     simple: [2, 3]
857:     complex: [5, 10]
858: ```
859: 
860: `/scripts/variant_detector.py`:
861: ```python
862: import yaml
863: 
864: class VariantDetector:
865:     def __init__(self, config_path: str):
866:         with open(config_path) as f:
867:             self.config = yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
868: 
869:     def should_generate_variants(self, request: str, complexity: int) -> bool:
870:         keywords = self.config['variant_triggers']['explicit_keywords']
871:         if any(kw in request.lower() for kw in keywords):
872:             return True
873: 
874:         threshold = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['complexity_threshold']
875:         if complexity >= threshold:
876:             signals = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['uncertainty_signals']
877:             return any(s in request.lower() for s in signals)
878:         return False
879: ```
880: 
881: **Why better:** Dynamic config loading, easier maintenance, schema validation possible
882: 
883: ---
884: 
885: ## 7. PYTHON SCRIPT INTEGRATION
886: 
887: ### When to Use Python for Logic
888: 
889: **Use Python scripts when**:
890: - Procedural logic (workflows, algorithms)
891: - Complex conditionals (multi-step decisions)
892: - Data transformation (processing, validation)
893: - API integration (external services)
894: - File operations (reading, parsing, generating)
895: 
896: ### Type Hints and Docstring Standards
897: 
898: **Always include**:
899: - Type hints for parameters and return values
900: - Google-style docstrings (Args, Returns, Raises, Examples)
901: - Dataclasses for structured data
902: 
903: **Example**:
904: ```python
905: from dataclasses import dataclass
906: from pathlib import Path
907: 
908: @dataclass
909: class ValidationResult:
910:     is_valid: bool
911:     errors: list[str]
912: 
913: def validate_config(config_path: Path) -> ValidationResult:
914:     """
915:     Validate configuration file.
916: 
917:     Args:
918:         config_path: Path to YAML config file
919: 
920:     Returns:
921:         ValidationResult with status and errors
922: 
923:     Raises:
924:         FileNotFoundError: If config doesn't exist
925:     """
926:     if not config_path.exists():
927:         raise FileNotFoundError(f"Config not found: {config_path}")
928:     # Validation logic
929:     return ValidationResult(is_valid=True, errors=[])
930: ```
931: 
932: ### Unit Testing Requirements
933: 
934: **Every Python script must have tests**:
935: - Naming: `test_[script_name].py` in `/tests/` directory
936: - Coverage: ≥80% line coverage
937: - Framework: pytest
938: 
939: **Example**:
940: ```python
941: import pytest
942: from scripts.config_validator import validate_config
943: 
944: def test_validate_success(tmp_path):
945:     config = tmp_path / "config.yaml"
946:     config.write_text("config:\n  threshold: 5")
947:     result = validate_config(config)
948:     assert result.is_valid
949: 
950: def test_validate_missing_file():
951:     with pytest.raises(FileNotFoundError):
952:         validate_config(Path("nonexistent.yaml"))
953: ```
954: 
955: ### Import and Reference Patterns
956: 
957: **Python import order**: Standard library → Third-party → Local
958: 
959: **Markdown references**:
960: ```markdown
961: **See also:** [script_name.py](../scripts/script_name.py), [config.yaml](../assets/config.yaml)
962: ```
963: 
964: ### Example: Workflow Decision Logic
965: 
966: **❌ BEFORE** (text decision tree):
967: ```markdown
968: IF "$quick": use quick mode (5 rounds)
969: IF "$ticket": use ticket mode (10 rounds)
970: OTHERWISE: use interactive mode
971: ```
972: 
973: **✅ AFTER** (Python with type safety):
974: 
975: `/scripts/workflow_router.py`:
976: ```python
977: from typing import Literal
978: from dataclasses import dataclass
979: 
980: WorkflowMode = Literal["quick", "ticket", "interactive"]
981: 
982: @dataclass
983: class WorkflowDecision:
984:     mode: WorkflowMode
985:     depth_rounds: int
986: 
987: def route_workflow(request: str) -> WorkflowDecision:
988:     """Route request to appropriate workflow."""
989:     if '$quick' in request.lower():
990:         return WorkflowDecision("quick", 5)
991:     if '$ticket' in request.lower():
992:         return WorkflowDecision("ticket", 10)
993:     return WorkflowDecision("interactive", 10)
994: ```
995: 
996: `/tests/test_workflow_router.py`:
997: ```python
998: def test_quick_mode():
999:     assert route_workflow("$quick fix").mode == "quick"
1000: 
1001: def test_default_mode():
1002:     assert route_workflow("help me").mode == "interactive"
1003: ```
1004: 
1005: **Why better:** Type-safe with Literal, testable, structured with dataclass
1006: 
1007: ---
1008: 
1009: ## 8. STANDARD STRUCTURE TEMPLATE
1010: 
1011: ### Complete Skill Directory Structure
1012: 
1013: **Path:** `.skilled/skills/` (singular, not `skills` or `openskills`)
1014: 
1015: ```
1016: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
1017: ├── SKILL.md                    # Main skill file (Level 2 in progressive disclosure)
1018: ├── references/                 # Deep-dive technical documentation (Level 3)
1019: │   ├── workflow-name.md        # Multi-phase workflows with checkpoints (kebab-case)
1020: │   ├── patterns-library.md     # Before/after code patterns (kebab-case)
1021: │   ├── debugging-guide.md      # Systematic troubleshooting (kebab-case)
1022: │   └── quick-reference.md      # Commands, shortcuts, checklists (kebab-case)
1023: ├── scripts/                    # Executable Python logic
1024: │   ├── mode_detection.py       # Procedural logic, algorithms
1025: │   ├── workflow_router.py      # Decision logic
1026: │   ├── config_validator.py     # Data transformation
1027: │   └── __init__.py             # Package initialization
1028: ├── assets/                     # Configuration and data files
1029: │   ├── workflow-configs/       # YAML workflow definitions
1030: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
1031: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
1032: │   ├── mappings/               # YAML mapping data
1033: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
1034: │   │   └── mode-recognition.yaml
1035: │   └── templates/              # Markdown/code templates
1036: │       ├── template-name.md
1037: │       └── component-template.tsx
1038: └── tests/                      # Unit and integration tests
1039:     ├── test_mode_detection.py
1040:     ├── test_workflow_router.py
1041:     ├── test_config_validator.py
1042:     └── __init__.py
1043: ```
1044: 
1045: ### Directory Purposes
1046: 
1047: **SKILL.md** (Required): Overview, workflow (3-5 steps), rules. Target: <200 lines
1048: 
1049: **references/** (Optional): Detailed workflows, patterns, debugging. Target: 500-3000 lines/file. **All authored filenames must use kebab-case.**
1050: 
1051: **scripts/** (Optional): Python logic - procedural, routing, validation. Requires type hints, tests
1052: 
1053: **assets/** (Optional): YAML configs, workflow definitions, templates, mappings
1054: 
1055: **tests/** (Required if scripts/ exists): Unit tests with ≥80% coverage, pytest, `test_[name].py`
1056: 
1057: ### When to Create Each Directory
1058: 
1059: | Directory     | Create When                                                     | Don't Create When                           |
1060: | ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
1061: | `references/` | Content >200 lines, multi-phase workflows, systematic debugging | Simple skills <200 lines total              |
1062: | `scripts/`    | Python logic extracted from markdown, reusable functions        | Pure documentation, no executable logic     |
1063: | `assets/`     | YAML configs, templates, structured data                        | No configuration data, inline examples only |
1064: | `tests/`      | `scripts/` directory exists                                     | No Python scripts to test                   |
1065: 
1066: ### Integration Pattern
1067: 
1068: **How components work together:**
1069: - SKILL.md references scripts: `[workflow_router.py](./scripts/workflow_router.py)`
1070: - Scripts load configs: `yaml.safe_load(f"../assets/config.yaml")`
1071: - Tests verify scripts: `assert route_workflow("input").mode == "expected"`
1072: - Markdown links to all: "See [script.py](../scripts/), [config.yaml](../assets/)"

# SKILL.md File Templates - Creation Guide

Templates for creating SKILL.md files with proper structure, frontmatter, and required sections.

---

## 1. OVERVIEW

### Purpose of SKILL.md Files

SKILL.md files define AI agent skills - reusable capabilities that extend an agent's functionality for specific domains or workflows. A well-crafted SKILL.md:

- **Triggers automatically** when relevant patterns are detected
- **Guides the agent** through specialized workflows
- **Maintains consistency** across conversations
- **Encodes expertise** in specific domains

### Template Overview

This guide provides **one comprehensive SKILL template** (Section 3) that covers all skill types from simple single-purpose tools to complex multi-mode orchestrators.

**The template is flexible:**
- **Simple skills**: Use required core sections only (WHEN TO USE, SMART ROUTING, HOW IT WORKS, RULES, REFERENCES)
- **Skills with bundled resources**: Say in Section 2 what selects the skill and what it loads first, and put the router in the sibling `ROUTER.md`. Use `references/`, `assets/`, and `scripts/`
- **Multi-mode skills**: Expand WHEN TO USE and HOW IT WORKS sections by mode
- **All skills**: Section 2 (SMART ROUTING) is required: 8 to 12 non-blank lines of plain prose

**Target size**: 800-2000 lines for SKILL.md (<5k words total)

**Examples**:
- Simple: Unit test generator, documentation formatter (no bundled resources)
- Moderate: API client, specialized code reviewer (with references and assets)
- Complex: Workflow orchestrator, document quality pipeline (multi-mode with extensive resources)

### Progressive Disclosure Principle

SKILL.md architecture follows progressive disclosure:

1. **Metadata** (YAML frontmatter) - Always in context (~100 words)
2. **SKILL.md body** - When skill activates (<5k words)
3. **Bundled resources** - Loaded as needed (unlimited size)

**Critical**: Keep SKILL.md <5k words. Move detailed content to `references/`, `scripts/`, or `assets/`.

### Document Type Requirements

**Enforcement Level**: STRICT (SKILL.md files require perfect structure)

**Required Elements**:
- ✅ YAML frontmatter with required fields
- ✅ H1 title with subtitle
- ✅ Numbered H2 sections (ALL CAPS, integers only, never a letter suffix such as `2b.`)
- ✅ Section separators (`---`)
- ✅ No table of contents (forbidden in SKILL.md)

**Quality Targets**:
- Structure: 100/100
- Content quality: High (AI-evaluated)
- Overall: High (human/AI judgment)

## 10. RENAME-HEAVY MERGE VERIFICATION

Merging a branch that renamed thousands of files (e.g. a `git mv`-driven spec-folder reorg/renumber) into a main that has diverged is a distinct, high-risk operation.

- The tree can end up *correct* while the working directory and `ls` *look* broken.
- git's own rename detection can silently give up at scale.

This section codifies rename-heavy merge verification. Scoped staging for that operation lives in [commit-workflows.md](./commit-workflows.md) §3 Step 6.

### 10.1 Before the merge — prove disjointness

A rename-heavy merge is conflict-free only if the two sides changed *disjoint* sets of files since their merge base. Verify this BEFORE merging:

```bash
BASE=$(git merge-base main reorg-branch)

# Files each side changed since the common ancestor
git diff --name-only "$BASE" main          | sort -u > /tmp/changed-main.txt

```markdown
□ merge-base computed; comm -12 of each side's changed files is EMPTY (disjoint)  [§10.1]
□ merge run with raised merge.renameLimit / diff.renameLimit; no "rename detection skipped" warning  [§10.2]
□ git ls-files <old> == 0 for every renamed-away folder (not `ls`)  [§10.3]
□ gitignored ghost folders identified and cleaned from working tree (not in commit)  [§10.3]
□ renames recorded as R status, not D+A churn  [§10.4]
□ scoped-staging discipline applied if the tree held unrelated WIP  [commit-workflows.md §3 Step 7]
```

The two are not interchangeable, and the difference is the point: creating a branch on origin publishes a name other machines will fetch, so it takes an approval that names what is being created. A bare `1` never creates.

A second variable, `SPECKIT_SKIP_PREPUSH_NAMING`, used to skip a naming-grammar gate that ran beside this one. ## 6. OPERATOR-FACING BEHAVIOR

A blocked push prints the exact retry command:

```
BLOCKED: push to '<branch>' on origin needs explicit permission for this push.
This repo asks before every push to a branch outside the remote allowlist
(built in: main, skilled/v*; extend via
  .skilled/skills/sk-git/scripts/remote-branch-allowlist.txt).
If the operator has approved THIS push, retry with:
  SPECKIT_ALLOW_REMOTE_PUSH=1 git push ...
```

This applies identically whether the push was issued by Claude or typed at a real terminal — the hook cannot tell the two apart, so both get the same safety net and the same one-line fix.

tree legible as a few clean folders instead of a per-skill pile. `{slug}` is a

- **Directory**: `<repo-root>/.worktrees/{NNN}-{slug}` — e.g.

- **`{NNN}`** is a 3-digit zero-padded **per-namespace** counter (001..999).
  `worktrees/` and `branches/` each number independently, strictly sequential,
  never skipped or reused — a `worktrees/003` and a `branches/003` may coexist,

  shared common git dir and seeds each namespace's max from its stored high-water
  mark, every matching local + remote ref, and (for `worktrees/`) every registered
  worktree basename, so a partial scan can never reissue a live number. Never
  hand-compute `{NNN}`.
